story: Two brothers, Kulbob (the younger) and Manub (the older), lived on Karkar Island. Kulbob was a hunter and carver; Manub was a fisherman. Conflict began when Manub's wife persuaded Kulbob to carve his identifying pattern on her thighs in exchange for his missing arrow. Manub interpreted this as adultery. Fighting broke out between the followers of the two brothers. Kulbob escaped by turning into a lizard and hiding inside a ngaul tree. The tree was cut down and fell into a bay. From the fallen tree, Kulbob built a great canoe and smaller craft. In one version, a large ship with a funnel and European goods rose from the water. Kulbob loaded the vessel with valuable artifacts, animals, and food plants, released beautiful young people from bamboo containers, and sailed away. When Manub tried to imitate him, his canoes sank and their crews drowned. In some versions, the younger brother offered the older brother a choice between local and European goods; the older brother chose bows, arrows, canoes, taro, and pigs rather than firearms, dinghies, rice, and canned food — explaining why Europeans possess ships, guns, and manufactured wealth while local people retained older technologies. The capsized canoe became Karkar Island, and its outrigger became Bagbag Island. Kulbob's travels also distributed practical knowledge: he rewarded a man named Buroi with gifts of food plants, house-building plans, canoe-building plans, and cooking instructions, explaining how skills and resources came to be unevenly distributed across the region.
